evidence.quote: The Financial Industry Business Ontology (FIBO) defines the sets of things that are of interest in financial business applications and the ways that those things can relate to one another.
FIBO provides a common, semantically precise, and machine-readable way to describe financial concepts and their relationships across systems, business units, companies, and supply chains.
has sub-classes condition precedent, contractual commitment, contractual definition, non-binding term

items.name: Symboleo
items.what_it_models: Formal specification language for legal contracts: a Domain section declares Roles, Assets and Events; a Contract Body declares Obligations and Powers each with a trigger, debtor role, creditor role, antecedent and consequent. Lifecycle states are formalised in temporal logic; supports model-checking and Hyperledger smart-contract code generation.

evidence.quote: Symboleo is a formal contract specification language developed by Contract Specification and Modelling (CSM) Lab at Univeristy of Ottawa EECS department.
obligations have a name, a trigger(_optional_), two roles, an antecedent and a consequent
powers have a name, a trigger(_optional_), two roles, an antecedent and a consequent

items.name: OASIS LegalXML eContracts v1.0
items.what_it_models: Generic hierarchical XML schema for contract documents (negotiated, template, standard-form, click-through); defines a recursive item/block tree with field elements for variable substitution enabling document assembly. Three content-structure patterns (tight/standard/loose) control block/item nesting. Metadata at contract and clause level.

evidence.quote: The eContracts Schema is intended to describe the generic hierarchical structure of a wide range of contract documents.
embedded data values to support variables substitution in contract preparation

The primary use of the eContracts Schema will be to facilitate the maintenance of precedent or template contract documents and contract terms by persons who wish to use them to create new contract documents with automated tools.

items.name: Open Contracting Data Standard (OCDS)
items.what_it_models: Public-procurement contracting processes as structured JSON data uniquely identified by an OCID; models parties, planning, tender, award, contract and implementation stages in a release/record structure. JSON Schema with CSV conversion. Focused on government procurement; not general private-law contracts.

evidence.quote: The Open Contracting Data Standard (OCDS) enables disclosure of data and documents at all stages of the contracting process by defining a common data model.
Version 1.1.5 (latest)
The OCDS defines a unique contracting process as all the actions aimed at implementing one or more contracts.

items.name: Institutional Grammar 2.0 (IG 2.0 / ADICO)
items.what_it_models: Institutional statements encoding rules, norms and strategies via ADICO syntax: Attribute (who), Deontic (may/must/must-not), aIm (action), Conditions (when/where), Or-else (consequence); distinguishes strategies (AIC), norms (ADIC) and rules (ADICO)

evidence.quote: IG 2.0 is a specification that aims at facilitating the encoding of policy to meet varying analytical objectives.
it revises the grammar with respect to comprehensiveness, flexibility, and specificity by offering multiple levels of expressiveness (IG Core, IG Extended, IG Logico).

items.name: LegalRuleML Core Specification V1.0
items.what_it_models: Legal normative rules with obligations, permissions, prohibitions, defeasibility, temporal management, jurisdiction, and isomorphic mapping between rules and legal text; XML-schema and RelaxNG on top of RuleML 1.02

evidence.quote: extend RuleML with formal features specific to legal norms
able to represent the particularities of the legal normative rules with a rich, articulated, and meaningful mark-up language

items.name: Catala
items.what_it_models: Legislative text encoded as executable algorithms using prioritised default logic; literate programming pairs each statutory article with its formal implementation; compiler correctness proved in F*

evidence.quote: a new programming language that we specifically designed to allow a straightforward and systematic translation of statutory law into an executable implementation.
Catala aims to bring together lawyers and programmers through a shared medium, which together they can understand, edit and evolve.
adapted for socio-fiscal legislative literate programming

items.name: LKIF Core Legal Ontology
items.what_it_models: Legal concepts in OWL-DL/SWRL across 15 modules: norms, acts, roles, legal persons, rights, powers, processes, and expressions; foundational ontology for legal knowledge systems

evidence.quote: The LKIF core legal ontology is a library of ontologies relevant for the legal domain. It consists of 15 modules, each of which describes a set of closely related concepts from both legal and commonsense domains.
LKIF builds on and uses the Web Ontology Language (OWL) for representing concepts
The core of LKIF consists of a combination of OWL-DL and SWRL.

items.name: Blawx
items.what_it_models: Declarative logic encoding of legal rules with defeasible reasoning, open-world assumption, hypothetical reasoning, and natural language explanations; s(CASP) constraint answer-set programming as reasoner

evidence.quote: an open source, user-friendly, web-based declarative logic knowledge representation tool designed specifically for encoding, testing and using rules.
A reasoner built on SWI-Prolog and s(CASP) for answering questions with explanations

items.name: Symboleo
items.governing_body: Contract Specification and Modelling Lab, University of Ottawa
items.what_it_models: Contracts as structured collections of obligations and powers over parties and assets, with formal semantics in statecharts and temporal logic; targets normative monitoring and smart contract generation

evidence.quote: a structured and machine-readable language for specifying contractual obligations, powers, and domain concepts
Obligations: indicate duties one role owes another, triggered by specific conditions. Each obligation has an antecedent and a consequent legal position
Powers: allow a role to instantiate, change, suspend, or terminate obligations when conditions are met

items.name: Marlowe
items.what_it_models: Financial contracts as executable, formally verified programs on blockchain; time-bounded exchanges of funds between parties with conditional branching, embedded in Haskell DSL

evidence.quote: Marlowe-Cardano is an implementation of Marlowe for the Cardano blockchain, built on top of Plutus.
Marlowe contracts are unique due to their foundation in peer-reviewed research. Formal proofs, extensive testing, and analysis tools provide strong assurances for the safety of Marlowe contracts.

items.name: Stipula
items.governing_body: Crafa, Laneve, Sartor (University of Bologna / University of Padova)
items.what_it_models: Legal contracts as interaction protocols between parties with permissions, obligations, prohibitions, and asset transfers; formal semantics drawn from process calculi and concurrency theory

evidence.quote: agreement, permissions, violations and obligations
based on a small set of abstractions that correspond to common patterns in legal contracts

items.name: Composing Contracts: An Adventure in Financial Engineering (Peyton Jones & Eber)
items.what_it_models: Financial contracts as algebraic combinators with compositional denotational semantics; enables algebraic composition, decomposition, and valuation of contract terms; foundational paper for contract DSLs including Marlowe

evidence.quote: We introduce a combinator library that allows us to describe such contracts precisely, and a compositional denotational semantics that says what such contracts are worth.

Financial and insurance contracts do not sound like promising territory for functional programming and formal semantics, but in fact we have discovered that insights from programming languages bear directly on the complex subject of describing and valuing a large class of contracts.

items.name: ACTUS (Algorithmic Contract Types Unified Standards)
items.governing_body: ACTUS Financial Research Foundation / ACTUS Users Association
items.what_it_models: Financial contracts as algorithmic cash-flow generators using standardised contract types; separates contractual logic (the known) from risk factors (the unknown); covers 32+ contract types from annuities to credit default swaps

evidence.quote: a global standard for the consistent representation of financial instruments
open, royalty-free standards for the combined data and algorithmic representation of financial contracts
ACTUS is based on a modeling paradigm, in which standardized Contract Types (CTs) are the granular building blocks

items.name: LogiKEy Workbench (deontic logics in Isabelle/HOL)
items.governing_body: Benzmüller et al. (Free University Berlin / University of Luxembourg)
items.what_it_models: Multiple deontic logics (Standard Deontic Logic, Dyadic, I/O logic, STIT), normative theories and selected legal texts encoded in Isabelle/HOL via shallow semantic embeddings; supports proof-assistant-validated legal and ethical reasoning

evidence.quote: A framework and methodology---termed LogiKEy---for the design and engineering of ethical reasoners, normative theories and deontic logics is presented.
Formal encodings of multiple deontic logics, logic combinations, deontic paradoxes and normative theories in the higher-order proof assistant system Isabelle/HOL

items.name: Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL)
items.governing_body: Governatori et al. (CSIRO / Griffith University) and research community
items.what_it_models: Legal norms as defeasible rules with deontic operators for obligation, permission and impermissibility; exceptions override general rules via superiority relations; combines defeasible logic with standard deontic logic for practical normative reasoning

evidence.quote: transformation into Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL)
it is obligatory that p
it is permissible that p

fits.rationale: AKN is the OASIS international standard for legislative document structure, providing FRBR-based URI naming (FRBRuri, FRBRthis, FRBRdate) for point-in-time law identification. It is the cross-jurisdictional alignment layer that USLM (US) and e-Gov (Japan) both overlap with, enabling uniform law citation across jurisdictions (cq-002). Its act/article/portion model also informs the source sublayer of clause decomposition (cq-001). Version 1.0 is the current OASIS Standard; v2.0/AKN 3.1 was in public comment at run time.

USLM 2.1.0 is the authoritative GPO XML schema for the US Code, bills, resolutions, and public laws. It directly provides versioned, addressable US federal primary law required by cq-002. The GitHub-hosted schema is the definitive source for positive-law codification structure and stylistic variants used by Congress.

The Japan Digital Agency's e-Gov XML schema (XMLSchemaForJapaneseLaw_v3) and API v2 (released 2025-03-14) provide full-text retrieval, article-level access, amendment history, and point-in-time versioning for Japanese statutes, cabinet orders, and ministerial ordinances. This is the authoritative structured source for Japanese primary law (cq-002), directly relevant to the GK entity's governing jurisdiction.

UK law is outside the primary jurisdiction scope (Japan, Delaware, US federal). However, CLML v2.6 is the most mature public implementation of historical-version access at article level with a documented API, and serves as a design reference for how to implement point-in-time versioning for our Japan and US law layers. Retained as a reference pattern, not as a data source.

Formex is specific to EU Official Journal publications. EU law is outside the primary jurisdiction scope, and the potential Austrian entity was not included in the charter's primary scope. Formex provides no coverage for Japan, Delaware, or US federal law and is therefore not relevant to any charter need.

docassemble's guided interview and conditional-branching document assembly pattern (interview → question blocks → template → DOCX/PDF) is the proven architecture for drafting from structured inputs (cq-005). However, docassemble is a UI layer without the typed semantic data model the charter requires; borrow the interview-driven assembly and conditional logic patterns rather than adopting it as a model layer.

Cicero is the Linux Foundation runtime that parses natural-language contract templates bound to Concerto typed data models, extracts structured clause data, and executes clause logic against JSON event payloads. This directly realises clause-as-structured-object (cq-001), obligation execution (cq-003), template-driven drafting (cq-005), and lifecycle event processing (cq-011). Apache-2.0 licence and open governance make it suitable as a foundational tool layer.

Catala compiles annotated legislative text into verified executable algorithms using prioritised default logic, with compiler correctness proved in F*. Its literate-programming approach keeps legal text and formal model in sync. This directly realises cq-003 (obligations as executable rules with conditions and breach consequences), cq-014 (formal semantics for statutory obligations), and cq-015 (scope definitions and priority rules provide algebraic composition of legal defaults). Apache-2.0, active, Inria-maintained.

OpenFisca's Variable/Entity/Formula/Period model and JSON/Python API encode computable rules with parameter sensitivity analysis, applicable to cost-plus pricing and transfer-pricing computation (cq-008) and rule execution (cq-003). However, OpenFisca is primarily scoped to socio-fiscal microsimulation, not contract clause semantics; borrow its computation architecture and period-aware formula model rather than adopting it as a contract model layer.

LexNLP provides NLP extraction patterns for monetary amounts, dates, citations, courts, and regulations from unstructured legal text — relevant for drafting from meeting notes (cq-005) and clause review (cq-006). LexNLP is dormant since November 2022 (v2.3.0, no subsequent releases confirmed); borrow its extraction logic and legal-abbreviation-aware sentence parsing as patterns to adapt, not as a live dependency to adopt.

python-redlines generates native Word tracked-change redlines (insertions, deletions, moves, structural differences) from two .docx files. This directly implements the Word-redline negotiation workflow required by cq-006. Active, MIT-licensed, and the only verified open-source package providing this specific capability.

docxtpl's Jinja2-in-DOCX template engine projects the typed contract data model into the Word format counterparties expect, directly realising the 'PDF is only a projection' principle of cq-001 and template-driven drafting (cq-005). Lightweight, LGPL-licensed, widely used in legal document pipelines, and actively maintained.

WeasyPrint converts HTML/CSS using CSS Paged Media into paginated PDF. In the target architecture, the HTML layer is a structured rendering of the contract data model, making WeasyPrint the PDF-projection step required by cq-001. BSD-licensed and actively maintained.

Common Paper provides NDA, Cloud Service Agreement, and Professional Services Agreement under CC BY 4.0 with a Cover Page + Standard Terms two-part structure. This parametric form design (variable Cover Page, stable Standard Terms incorporated by reference) is the pattern for drafting from a template (cq-005) and reviewing against a known position (cq-006). The Professional Services Agreement is directly applicable to services between the GK and C-corp (cq-008 context).

Bonterms targets the same B2B agreement types as Common Paper (NDA, Cloud Terms, PSA) and is a direct substitute. Its additional AI Standard Clauses and UK/EU jurisdiction variants add coverage beyond Common Paper's scope. Borrow the AI clauses and cross-jurisdictional term variants as supplementary content rather than adopting a competing primary form standard.

The YC Post-Money SAFE is the industry-standard instrument for pre-seed startup financing, with variants for valuation cap, discount rate, and MFN. It directly provides the canonical form for cq-010 (SAFEs and founder stock). Freely available from Y Combinator and widely accepted by investors and counsel in the US and internationally.

NVCA Model Legal Documents (October 2025) are the industry standard for venture capital financing and Delaware corporate governance. They cover Certificate of Incorporation, Stock Purchase Agreement, Investors' Rights Agreement, Voting Agreement, Board Consent, and Stockholder Consent — directly serving cq-009 (corporate governance instruments for the C-corp) and cq-010 (startup financing preferred-stock mechanics).

Cooley GO generates NVCA and YC SAFE documents (both already adopted) as parametric outputs, demonstrating how Cover Page + Standard Terms can be realised as a generator. Useful as a reference for parametric form generation design (cq-005), but it is a proprietary tool whose documents are derived from NVCA/SAFE. No distinct content or open schema to adopt beyond what is already covered.

IPA 情報システム・モデル取引・契約書 (Second Edition + Agile Edition) are the Japanese government-endorsed model contracts for IT system development. They directly govern services between a Japanese technology provider (the GK) and a user company under commissioned-development, maintenance/operations, and agile frameworks (cq-008, cq-009). The most authoritative Japanese-language IT contract templates available and the baseline for services agreement drafting in Japan (cq-005).

PROV-O (W3C Recommendation 2013) provides the OWL ontology for expressing provenance — entities, activities, agents, derivation chains (prov:wasDerivedFrom), and attribution (prov:wasAttributedTo). It is the standard model for expressing lineage of clauses back to statutory sources (cq-001: source sublayer), and for attributing and tracing primary law references to their origins (cq-002). Its prov:Bundle supports named provenance graphs for each instrument version.

GLEIF LEI (ISO 17442:2020) provides globally unique, persistent 20-character codes for legal entities with Level 1 (entity identity) and Level 2 (ownership/relationship structure) data freely accessible via the Global LEI Index. Using LEI codes as canonical party identifiers ensures unambiguous identification of the GK, the C-corp, and counterparties in obligations (cq-003: who bears which obligation) and authority records (cq-004: which entity is being bound).

ELI provides HTTP URIs and OWL metadata (eli:LegalResource, eli:LegalExpression) for EU and national legislation using FRBR-based point-in-time versioning. EU law is outside primary scope, but ELI's ontology is the closest formal model to what is needed for law citation metadata and directly informed the URN:LEX design. Reference for provenance design of Japan and US federal law sources.

URN:LEX (RFC 9676) provides persistent, location-independent, jurisdiction-neutral identifiers for sources of law using the FRBR Work/Expression/Manifestation/Item hierarchy with jurisdiction/work/expression partition-ids. As the IETF-published specification for law URNs across any jurisdiction, it is the URI scheme for citing Japanese, US federal, and Delaware primary law with version precision — directly serving the 'versioned, addressable primary law with lineage' requirement of cq-002.

W3C VC Data Model v2.0 (Recommendation 2025-05-15) provides tamper-evident, cryptographically verifiable credentials for claims about subjects. For cq-004, a VC can attest that a named individual holds authority to bind a specific entity (identified by LEI) for a specified scope. The credentialSubject, issuer, validFrom, validUntil, and termsOfUse fields provide the structural slots for an authority grant credential, subject to additional schema work to model scope and monetary limits.

W3C DID v1.1 (Candidate Recommendation, 2026-03-05) provides cryptographically verifiable, decentralized identifiers for parties and documents — the identity layer that W3C VC depends on for issuer and subject identification (cq-004). Borrow the DID resolution pattern for identity infrastructure. DID v1.1 has not reached full Recommendation status at run time; DID method selection for our specific use case requires further evaluation before full adoption.

DOI / ISO 26324:2025 provides persistent, citable, resolvable identifiers for intellectual content objects. URN:LEX and AKN FRBR URIs are more appropriate for primary law, and PROV-O handles document lineage. DOI is the appropriate citation identifier for published academic papers and standards cited in our model (e.g., Composing Contracts, Catala papers), but not the primary identifier system for instruments or legislation.

DCMI Terms provides lightweight provenance properties (dct:provenance, dct:isVersionOf, dct:replaces, dct:creator, dct:created) that are a practical complement to PROV-O for standard document metadata. Borrow the dc:terms vocabulary for bibliographic metadata on instruments (creator, date, version lineage) while PROV-O handles structural derivation graphs. The two vocabularies are explicitly aligned in the scan relator output.

CUAD's 41 clause categories — including Change of Control, IP Ownership Assignment, Governing Law, Most Favored Nation, and Termination For Convenience — provide an expert-validated taxonomy for the clause types we need to identify in review (cq-006), track (cq-011), and query across a portfolio (cq-012). The IP Ownership Assignment category directly supports cq-007. The 510-contract, 13,000+ annotation corpus is the primary training data source for clause extraction models. CC BY 4.0.

LEDGAR's 100,000 provisions across 12,000+ topic labels provides a broader provision-classification taxonomy than CUAD's 41 categories. Its multi-label approach informs how a single clause can serve multiple legal purposes. Borrow as supplementary training data and evidence that provision classification generalises beyond CUAD — CUAD is adopted as the primary taxonomy.

MAUD provides 47,000+ expert annotations on 152 merger agreements covering M&A deal points (change-of-control, MAC, representations and warranties, termination rights). Directly relevant for change-of-control clause queries in cq-012 and for reviewing acquisition documents in cq-006. Borrow as training data and as the M&A segment of the clause taxonomy.

ContractNLI provides document-level NLI labels (entailment/contradiction/not-mentioned) for 17 fixed hypotheses on 607 NDAs, supporting automated review of NDA clauses against a known position (cq-006). Borrow as the evaluation framework and training data for the NDA clause review component, where the hypothesis-testing model maps directly to our review-against-positions need.

ACORD provides 114 expert-annotated retrieval queries with 126,000+ ranked clause pairs (1–5 stars) for clause types including Limitation of Liability, Indemnification, Change of Control, and MFN. This is the only verified retrieval benchmark fully annotated by experts for contract drafting: it directly supports drafting from precedent (cq-005: find the closest matching precedent clause) and benchmarking our review models against market-standard clause quality (cq-006). CC BY 4.0.

SALI LMSS provides 18,000+ tagged concepts for classifying legal work by area of law, service type, industry, and player role, with stable IRIs for interoperability. As a matter-classification taxonomy rather than a contract data model, it is a reference for tagging portfolio instruments by area of law and enabling cross-system interoperability in cq-012 (portfolio querying for diligence). Not a clause-level or obligation-level model to adopt.

Pile of Law provides 256GB+ of legal pretraining data (US contracts, court opinions, legislation, regulations) for building or fine-tuning legal language models used in drafting (cq-005) and extraction. Borrow as a pretraining corpus for LLM components in the drafting pipeline. Note: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence restricts commercial use; this constraint must be tracked in any production deployment.

MCC provides 1M+ SEC Exhibit-10 material contracts (2000–2023) with ML-generated contract type labels, party identification, and EDGAR metadata. The scale and labelling make it the best open corpus for training contract-type classifiers and clause-extraction models for drafting from precedent (cq-005) and portfolio classification (cq-012). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 restricts commercial use.

LexGLUE is a multi-task legal NLP benchmark integrating LEDGAR, ContractNLI, and other datasets for standardised evaluation of legal language understanding. It is the reference for evaluating our clause extraction and review models against published baselines (cq-006). Informative for model evaluation design but not a data layer or tool to directly adopt.

MultiLegalPile covers 24 languages across 17 jurisdictions as a 689GB pretraining corpus, and is the largest available multilingual legal pretraining corpus. Although it lacks clause-level annotations, it is the primary resource for training Japanese-language legal NLP components required by cq-013. No verified Japanese-specific annotated corpus was found in any layer; MultiLegalPile is the best available foundation for Japanese language coverage. Licence not confirmed in scan; usage terms must be verified.

ODRL 2.2 (W3C Recommendation) provides Policy/Permission/Prohibition/Duty/Asset/Party/Constraint as the formal model for expressing usage rights and obligations over digital assets. It directly models IP licences (cq-007: who has what rights over which assets under what territorial/purpose constraints), obligations arising from rights grants (cq-003), and compositional policy structures (cq-015: policies can be combined, overridden, and checked). The Spatial constraint maps to the Japan vs RoW territorial split in the IP licensing layer.

SPDX 3.0.1 (Linux Foundation) is the standard for software package licence and copyright communication via SPDX-License-Identifier and LicenseExpression. Given that the GK owns software IP licensed to the C-corp, SPDX provides the mechanism for communicating licence terms and IP chain-of-title for every software component — directly serving cq-007 (IP rights, assignments, and software asset lineage).

ccREL is the domain-specific precursor to ODRL, mapping cc:permits/cc:requires/cc:prohibits to ODRL's Permission/Duty/Prohibition. Since ODRL is adopted as the IP rights model, ccREL is retained as a reference for understanding how CC-licensed content expresses rights in RDF. It adds no distinct capability beyond what ODRL covers for our IP model.

WIPO ST.96 v7.0 XML schemas cover IP data exchange between national IP offices across patents, trademarks, and designs. Relevant for reading and exchanging patent/trademark bibliographic data when the GK's IP portfolio is referenced in licence agreements (cq-007). Not a contract model to adopt; a reference for the XML structure of IP right records originating from national IP offices.

The USPTO Patent Assignment Dataset documents conveyance types (assignment, licence, security interest, merger) with assignor/assignee and date metadata for 10.5M+ transactions since 1970. Useful as a reference for the conveyance types to model in the IP rights layer (cq-007) and as empirical data for diligence research (cq-012). Not a standard to adopt as a model layer.

LCC defines Party/Creation/Place/Context with Right/RightsAssignment/Assertion/RightsConflict context types for linked-data IP rights trading. The RightsConflict type is conceptually useful for territorial split analysis (cq-007). However, the LCC consortium concluded initial work circa 2014–2016 and ODRL supersedes it as the active standard. Reference for conceptual design of the rights conflict entity only.

IPROnto (OWL-DL, 2003, dormant) modelled Agreements, Exploitation Rights, Moral Rights, and LegalEntity for DRM. The Exploitation Rights vs Moral Rights distinction is relevant to Japanese copyright law (where moral rights are inalienable), informing our IP rights ontology design for cq-007. Dormant and superseded by ODRL for active use; reference for the moral-rights design only.

MPEG-21 REL (ISO/IEC 21000-5:2004) defines Licence/Grant/Principal/Right/Resource/Condition, with Condition covering territory and payment obligations. Informative for the conceptual lineage of rights expression standards leading to ODRL. Reference only; the full normative text is paywalled and ODRL is the active standard for our IP rights layer.

DALICC extends ODRL with a licence-compatibility dependency graph (implies/contradicts/included-in relations between licence actions), enabling automated licence compatibility checking. This is directly applicable to checking whether IP licences can be combined or conflict (cq-015: algebraic checking of obligations), particularly across the Japan vs RoW territorial split in our IP rights layer (cq-007). Borrow the dependency-graph approach into our ODRL-based IP model.

Accord Project (Concerto typed data model, TemplateMark prose binding, TypeScript logic) is the active Apache-2.0 open standard for machine-executable contract templates under Linux Foundation governance. Concerto's Asset/Participant/Transaction/Event model is the primary data model layer for the contract system: it addresses clause-as-structured-object (cq-001), executable obligation logic (cq-003), template-driven drafting (cq-005), and lifecycle event processing (cq-011). Accord-project-cicero (the runtime) is also adopted; together they form one integrated layer.

ISDA CDM's TradeState/BusinessEvent lifecycle model defines how a contract's state evolves through events (execution, amendment, termination). This event-driven state machine pattern is directly applicable to obligation lifecycle tracking (cq-011: due dates, events, amendments) and obligation state evaluation (cq-003). Borrow the TradeState/BusinessEvent design for the obligation lifecycle layer. CDM is scoped to OTC derivatives and cannot be adopted wholesale for general private-law contracts.

FIBO's FND/Agreements/Contracts OWL-DL module provides formal definitions for Contract, ContractParty, ContractualCommitment, ContractualDefinition, ConditionPrecedent, and BreachOfContract. Borrowing this vocabulary grounds our contract type model with OWL semantics, enabling machine-checked reasoning over obligation structure (cq-003) and party roles (cq-004). Full FIBO adoption is overly broad; borrow the FND/Agreements/Contracts module vocabulary.

Symboleo's formal contract specification language models obligations (name, trigger, two roles, antecedent, consequent legal position) and powers in statechart/temporal logic semantics, supporting model-checking and smart-contract code generation. Its antecedent/consequent obligation structure (cq-003: conditions and breach consequences) and compositional obligation model (cq-015) are directly applicable design patterns. Borrow the obligation/power formalism and trigger/consequence structure; Symboleo is an academic language without production tooling or governance, so adopt the design rather than the runtime.

OASIS eContracts v1.0 (2007, dormant) is a hierarchical XML schema for contract documents with field/variable substitution — the historical precedent that Accord Project supersedes. It is the lineage reference for contract document schema design (cq-001) and confirms that the parametric document model predates the current generation of tools. No active use.

OCDS covers public-procurement contracting processes only (parties, tender, award, contract, implementation for government procurement). The charter scopes exclusively to private bilateral instruments for a two-entity technology group. OCDS provides no coverage for any charter need and its procurement-specific data model would be misleading to incorporate.

IG 2.0's ADICO syntax (Attribute/Deontic/aIm/Conditions/Or-else) provides a structured analytical framework for decomposing institutional statements into normative components. Borrowing this as an analytical annotation layer for contract clauses — labelling who, what modal, what action, under what conditions, with what consequence — directly supports clause decomposition (cq-003) and provides a bridge between natural-language clause text and formal normative representations (cq-014).

LegalRuleML Core v1.0 (OASIS Standard 2021) extends RuleML with deontic operators (Obligation, Permission, Prohibition), defeasibility, temporal management, jurisdiction, and isomorphic mapping between rules and legal text. It provides the XML-based normative rule markup layer for encoding contract obligations with formal semantics (cq-003, cq-014), and its defeasibility and SuborderList features support checking and combining norms with priority ordering (cq-015). An OASIS Standard with open governance.

LKIF Core provides a 15-module OWL-DL/SWRL legal ontology covering Norm, Action, Role, Agent, Process, Legal Person, Rights, and Powers. Borrowing its vocabulary grounds the obligation model (cq-003) and authority model (cq-004) in OWL semantics, enabling machine-checked reasoning over legal concepts. Its maintained status (CC BY 4.0 relicence on GitHub) supports ongoing reference. Use as a vocabulary layer, not as the primary data model.

Blawx uses s(CASP) constraint answer-set programming to evaluate defeasible legal rules with open-world assumption, hypothetical reasoning, and natural-language explanations. Its defeasible reasoning engine is applicable to evaluating obligation conditions and exceptions from clause-level rules (cq-003, cq-014). Borrow the s(CASP)/defeasible reasoning architecture (MIT-licensed, active); the Blockly visual interface is not required for the target system.

Marlowe implements the Composing Contracts combinator model (Pay/If/When/Case/Close) with formal verification. Its combinator vocabulary and denotational semantics demonstrate how financial contracts can be represented algebraically with machine-checkable proofs (cq-014, cq-015). Borrow the combinator vocabulary and compositional contract model for the financial instrument obligation layer. The Cardano blockchain dependency is irrelevant; take the language design independently.

Stipula models legal contracts via process calculi and concurrency theory, providing formal semantics for permissions, violations, obligations, and asset transfers with observational equivalence. Useful as a reference for the process-calculus approach to contract formal semantics (complementing Symboleo's statechart approach and Marlowe's combinator approach), informing our choice of formal model. No production implementation or standard body; academic reference only.

Peyton Jones and Eber's 'Composing Contracts: An Adventure in Financial Engineering' introduces the combinator library (zero/one/give/and/or/truncate/get/anytime/scale) and compositional denotational semantics that defines what contracts are worth. This is the foundational theory for algebraic obligation composition and decomposition (cq-015) and provides the Curry-Howard contract calculus basis for cq-014. Its open implementations (Marlowe) and commercial lineage (LexiFi) confirm the theory is industrially realisable. Adopting this theoretical framework as the algebraic contract layer.

ACTUS provides 32+ financial contract types as algorithmic cash-flow generators, separating contractual logic from market observables with royalty-free open standards. Its contract-type taxonomy and state-contingent event model are directly applicable to modelling payment obligations in services agreements (cost-plus payment schedules, cq-008) and tracking when cash-flow obligations fall due (cq-011). Borrow the contract-type taxonomy and event model for financial obligation tracking.

LogiKEy provides proof-assistant-validated encodings of multiple deontic logics (Standard Deontic Logic, Dyadic, I/O, STIT) in Isabelle/HOL via shallow semantic embeddings. It is a reference confirming that the formal semantics target of cq-014 (obligations as machine-checked propositions) is achievable with existing proof-assistant technology, and provides validated deontic logic encodings to consult when selecting the formal model. Not a production tool for our system.

Defeasible Deontic Logic formalises legal norms as defeasible rules with obligation/permission/impermissibility operators where exceptions override general rules via superiority relations. This framework directly handles the exception structure of legal obligations — a general statutory duty overridden by a specific contractual carve-out (cq-003). Borrow DDL's superiority/defeater structure as the exception-handling layer in the normative rule model. The theory is well-established; implementations (DR-Device, SPINdle) exist and Blawx (borrowed separately) provides an s(CASP) realisation.

open_findings.claim: Japan Corporate Number (法人番号 / hōjin bangō) is absent from the provenance layer. It is the NTA-assigned 13-digit identifier for every Japanese legal entity, used in all Japanese contracts, invoices, and regulatory filings — including those of the GK entity at the centre of this domain.
open_findings.evidence: Fetched https://www.houjin-bangou.nta.go.jp/en/index.html on 2026-09-21: 'The Corporate Number of each organization that has such number designated, and the name and the address of the head office or principal place of business of each organization that has registered its indications in English.' The Corporate Number is a 13-digit public identifier published by the National Tax Agency; 5.78 million entities are registered. The provenance layer adopts GLEIF LEI for global entity identification but contains no entry for the Japanese domestic identifier. Japanese counterparties, courts, and tax authorities use the Corporate Number, not the LEI, to identify a Japanese GK.

open_findings.claim: GLEIF vLEI (ISO 17442-3:2024) is absent from the fit decisions despite being a published ISO standard whose role-credential mechanism directly addresses the uncovered cq-004 signing-authority gap.
open_findings.evidence: GLEIF press release at https://www.gleif.org/en/newsroom/press-releases/iso-standardizes-gleif-s-pioneering-digital-organizational-identity-offering-with-publication-of-vlei-technical-standard (found in search, 2026-09-21): 'ISO 17442-3, defined and standardized the use of vLEIs as digital credentials across the global LEI ecosystem.' ISO catalogue entry https://www.iso.org/standard/85628.html confirms publication in 2024. The standard defines role credentials that 'bind persons and roles to an LEI; official roles follow ISO 5009.' The scan item was refused by verification because the scout's verbatim quotes became stale on a dynamically rendered GLEIF page — not because the standard does not exist. The fit table contains no entry for vLEI, leaving cq-004 (signing authority scope) with zero fit decisions despite this ISO standard existing.

open_findings.claim: Typst (Apache-2.0, v0.15.1, July 2026) is absent from the tooling layer. It is the current leading open-source structured-markup-to-PDF typesetting compiler with bidirectional text support directly relevant to Japanese-English bilingual instrument generation.
open_findings.evidence: Fetched https://typst.app/open-source/ on 2026-09-21: 'The Typst compiler is licensed under the permissive Apache-2.0 license.' 'The Typst compiler is the open-source software that translates your Typst markup to PDFs, images, and web pages.' Version 0.14 (June 2026) added PDF/UA-1 accessibility compliance, expanded PDF/A support, and improved bidirectional text layout — the last property directly relevant to cq-013 (Japanese-English bilingual instruments). Version 0.15.1 is the stable release as of July 2026. The tooling scan investigated Typst but excluded it citing 'insufficient verbatim quote from primary page' — a page-rendering artefact. WeasyPrint (adopted) operates on HTML/CSS input; Typst operates on structured markup input. They are complementary, not redundant.

open_findings.claim: Catala is claimed to directly realise cq-003 (given a contract clause, determine obligations and breach consequences) but Catala was designed for socio-fiscal legislative text and has no confirmed application to bilateral commercial contract clause semantics.
open_findings.evidence: The Catala GitHub page (https://github.com/CatalaLang/catala) describes it as 'adapted for socio-fiscal legislative literate programming.' The Catala paper (arxiv:2103.03198, fetched by scout) demonstrates it on French family benefits and US income tax. cq-003 concerns commercial contract clauses (obligations created by a clause, breach consequences). Commercial contracts are bilateral negotiated instruments whose structure is not analogous to statutory priority-exception hierarchies. Accord Project (also adopted for cq-003) is the correct tool: it executes typed contract templates against event payloads. Assigning Catala to cq-003 alongside Accord Project creates a false impression that either can execute commercial contract obligations interchangeably.

open_findings.claim: The meti-jpo-model-contracts scan claims version ver2.2 released 2025-04-25, but the GitHub repository shows v1.0; the ver2.2 version came from search result snippets after a 403 error on the METI press release page — making it unverified.
open_findings.evidence: Fetching https://github.com/meti-oi-startups/METI-JPO-Model-Contract on 2026-09-21 found the repository at version 1.0 with CC-BY-4.0 licence. The scout caveat states: 'METI ver2.2 press release page returned HTTP 403; version and date confirmed via METI search result snippets.' The item was refused by verification (verbatim quote not found). If the repository is v1.0 and ver2.2 is sourced only from a 403-blocked press release snippet, the version claim is unverified. Type modelers relying on the 2025-04-25 release date for Japanese IP licensing model contracts cannot verify it.

open_findings.claim: CUAD is claimed to directly support cq-007 (IP rights, fields of use, territories, Japan vs RoW) based on its 'IP Ownership Assignment' clause category — but CUAD only identifies whether such a clause is present and extracts its text span; it does not model fields of use, territorial splits, or sublicensing structures.
open_findings.evidence: The CUAD paper (arxiv:2103.06268, confirmed): the task is 'to highlight salient portions of a contract that are important for a human to review.' The 'IP Ownership Assignment' category is a span-extraction task: does this clause exist and where is it? CUAD contains no territorial-split annotation, no field-of-use annotation, no Japan-specific content, and no sublicensing parameter. cq-007 asks for formal representation of rights, fields of use, territories, and sublicensing across Japan vs rest-of-world. ODRL (adopted) provides the model for this; CUAD provides only a detection benchmark, not a parameter model.

open_findings.claim: Defeasible Deontic Logic is presented as a single borrowable item with one canonical URL, but DDL is a research area with multiple incompatible implementations and no canonical specification; the scan evidence spans two papers from different research groups.
open_findings.evidence: The scan's DDL item URL is arxiv:2506.08899 (Governatori et al. applied paper). The scan evidence also quotes from arxiv:2507.05519v8 (a distinct ASP-based normative reasoning paper). The scan caveat states: 'the field has multiple competing implementations (Governatori's DR-Device, SPINdle, defeasible reasoner extensions) none of which was confirmed as a primary standard via fetch.' Blawx (separately borrowed) already provides the s(CASP) realisation of defeasible reasoning over legal norms. A type modeler asked to 'borrow DDL' cannot do so without selecting a specific implementation; the map does not provide this disambiguation.

open_findings.claim: Symboleo appears as a verified first-class item in both the norms-rules scan and the contract-models scan, with no primary-layer designation resolved in the fits, leaving an orphaned duplicate entry in contract-models.
open_findings.evidence: The landscape-verification confirms Symboleo in verified_handles twice. The contract-models scan includes Symboleo as a full item (handle: symboleo, layer: contract-models, kind: specification). The landscape-fit table contains one entry for Symboleo: borrow under norms-rules (cq-003/cq-014/cq-015). No fit entry appears for the contract-models instance. A type modeler reading the contract-models scan as the authoritative data-model layer would conclude Symboleo belongs there — but the fit decision is exclusively in norms-rules, making the contract-models entry misleading.

open_findings.claim: SALI LMSS is placed in the clause-corpora layer, whose chartered question is 'clause taxonomies and labelled datasets for learning clause families, parameters and variation' — a question LMSS does not answer.
open_findings.evidence: The clause-corpora scan's own caveat states: 'SALI LMSS is a matter-classification taxonomy (areas of law, service types, industries) rather than a clause-level labelled corpus.' LMSS (https://sali.org/explore-the-standard/) assigns legal matter types to legal work — 'consistent language for describing key attributes of matters (e.g., Services, Areas of Law, Industry).' It provides no clause text, no clause labels, and no training data for clause extraction. The fit correctly assigns it as a reference for cq-012 (portfolio querying by area of law), confirming it belongs in a standards or tooling layer rather than clause-corpora.

open_findings.claim: The relation `cooley-go implements yc-safe` is not supported by scan evidence: Cooley GO produces a Cooley-authored SAFE variant, not the YC Combinator-published SAFE document.
open_findings.evidence: The cooley-go scan evidence (https://www.cooleygo.com/documents/incorporation-package-delaware/) shows 'SAFE' as a core concept. The yc-safe scan evidence (https://www.ycombinator.com/documents) states: 'Created at Y Combinator by Carolynn Levy in 2013' with version-numbered releases (Post-Money SAFE v1.1, v1.2). 'Implements' asserts that cooley-go faithfully produces the yc-safe. No scan evidence shows Cooley GO produces the YC-published SAFE document rather than its own Cooley-authored form. The correct relation is 'references' — Cooley GO references the SAFE concept, not the specific YC document.

open_findings.claim: The relation `composing-contracts-pj overlaps actus` (PJ&E as ACTUS's theoretical precursor) is not grounded in scan evidence; the ACTUS technical specification does not cite Peyton Jones & Eber, and the two use incompatible mathematical structures.
open_findings.evidence: Fetching https://www.actusfrf.org/techspecs on 2026-09-21 found no citation to Peyton Jones & Eber. The ACTUS methodology page (fetched by scout: https://www.actusfrf.org/methodology) describes contract types via 'contract term attributes' mapped to 'state variable algorithms.' PJ&E use algebraic combinators (zero, one, give, and, or, truncate). ACTUS uses typed parameter matrices (e.g., NotionalPrincipal, CycleOfInterestPayment, ContractDealDate). These are different mathematical structures. The relation evidence in landscape-relations says only that both 'decompose financial contracts algebraically' — an inference from background knowledge, not from any fetched scan content for either item.

open_findings.claim: The relation `gleif-lei overlaps w3c-vc-data-model` is an architectural inference not grounded in either item's scan evidence; the word 'can' in the evidence marks it as a possibility, not a documented specification.
open_findings.evidence: The relation evidence reads: 'W3C VC's credentialSubject can carry LEI codes as subject identifiers' (emphasis on 'can'). Neither the GLEIF LEI page (https://www.gleif.org/en/organizational-identity/introducing-the-legal-entity-identifier-lei/iso-17442-the-lei-code-structure, fetched by scout) nor the W3C VC Data Model v2.0 (https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/, fetched by scout) states this combination. The vLEI (ISO 17442-3) is the GLEIF specification that actually integrates with verifiable credentials — and it was refused by verification. An 'overlaps' relation requires documented shared concepts, not architectural plausibility.

open_findings.claim: The relation `dalicc profiles odrl-information-model` is duplicated in the landscape-relations claims array (appears at positions 3 and 18 with identical content), producing a misleading double-entry.
open_findings.evidence: The landscape-relations output lists: claim[3] = 'dalicc profiles odrl-information-model: DALICC is explicitly an ODRL-based vocabulary extending ODRL's Permission/Duty/Prohibition with a licence-compatibility dependency graph.' claim[18] = 'dalicc profiles odrl-information-model: DALICC is an ODRL-based vocabulary for data-asset licence clearance extending ODRL with a dependency graph encoding implies/contradicts/included-in relations between licence actions.' Both cite the same source (https://dalicc.github.io/). The relations array also contains two formal relation objects for this pair. One entry should be removed.

open_findings.claim: The relation `ledgar overlaps pile-of-law` asserts LEDGAR's annotated contracts are a labelled subset within Pile of Law, but no scan evidence confirms the specific LEDGAR contract sample is included in the Pile of Law corpus.
open_findings.evidence: The relation evidence is: LEDGAR 'annotates almost 100,000 provisions in over 60,000 contracts' from SEC EDGAR (https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.155/); Pile of Law lists 'EDGAR filings' as a core concept (https://huggingface.co/datasets/pile-of-law/pile-of-law). 'EDGAR filings' in Pile of Law covers the broad EDGAR database; LEDGAR draws from a specific 60,000-contract sample with specific preprocessing and annotation. Neither the LEDGAR paper nor the Pile of Law HuggingFace page confirms the specific LEDGAR contracts are present in Pile of Law. The overlap is plausible from the shared source but is not verified by scan evidence.

open_findings.claim: The LCC Rights Reference Model is listed with status 'unknown' but is effectively dormant: its sole scan evidence is a 2014 NISO article, and the scan itself notes the LCC consortium concluded its initial work circa 2014-2016.
open_findings.evidence: The scan evidence for lcc-rights-reference-model cites only https://www.niso.org/niso-io/2014/12/linked-content-coalition-framework-rights-management (a December 2014 article). The scan caveat states: 'The LCC consortium appears to have concluded its initial framework work circa 2014–2016.' No recent version, release, or active governance was found. A consortium that concluded its work over a decade ago with no subsequent releases is dormant, not 'unknown status.' The fit relegates it to a reference for the RightsConflict concept only — appropriate — but the status field should read dormant so type modelers do not investigate it expecting active governance.

uncovered_questions: cq-004 (signing authority scope): No verified item provides a formal data model for who may bind which entity, up to what monetary limit, under what governance constraints. W3C VC Data Model (adopted) provides the credential envelope and GLEIF LEI (adopted) identifies the entity, but the authority-scope structure — instrument type, monetary ceiling, governance approval required — is not modelled in any verified item. The refused gleif-vlei (GLEIF vLEI / ISO 17442-3:2024) would have provided verifiable role credentials linking individual to entity and role, partially closing this gap; its evidence did not survive verification.

cq-008 (cost-plus services and transfer-pricing): No verified standard form or data model specifically addresses cost-plus pricing formulas, invoice validation, or transfer-pricing rationale for intra-group services agreements between a Japanese GK and a Delaware C-corp. OpenFisca (borrowed) and Catala (adopted) provide the computational substrate for encoding such rules, but the domain-specific form or schema for Japanese IT services transfer pricing is absent. IPA model contracts (adopted) cover the structural form but not the financial mechanics.

cq-013 (bilingual document synchronization): No verified item addresses English/Japanese document synchronization, language-of-record semantics, or translation validation. MultiLegalPile (borrowed) provides Japanese-language legal pretraining data but no synchronization or validation model. This is a complete gap across all eight layers; building a bilingual clause model will require bespoke work without a standard to build on.

cq-009 (partial — Japanese GK governance): NVCA model documents (adopted) cover Delaware C-corp governance well, but no verified item provides model forms or a structured data model for 合同会社 member decisions, representative member authority designations, or GK operating agreement provisions. The refused meti-jpo-model-contracts would have partially addressed the Japanese IP/open-innovation dimension; GK-specific governance instruments remain uncovered.

cq-002 (partial — Delaware Code structured data): The scan explicitly confirmed that the Delaware Code is published in HTML and PDF only; no XML schema, bulk XML download, or structured API was found (recorded as not-found in law-markup scan). Delaware primary law cannot be ingested as versioned addressable structured data through any verified source. Third-party aggregators provide structured access but were not verified in this run.

cq-012 (partial — cross-contract portfolio query model): No verified item defines a query language or queryable data model for answering diligence questions across a contract portfolio (all change-of-control clauses, all IP assignments, all obligations due in a period). CUAD clause categories (adopted), SALI LMSS taxonomy (referenced), and ODRL policy expressions (adopted) collectively provide vocabulary, but the cross-contract query layer — a graph or document store exposing these as queryable dimensions — is not covered by any verified item.
